section.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
section.sectionRationale: Under a new empire, jealous officials trap the aged Daniel with a law against praying to anyone but the king. Daniel keeps praying openly toward Jerusalem, is thrown to the lions, and is delivered by God, who shuts the lions' mouths. The last court narrative crowns the theme of the first six chapters: God preserves His faithful servant in the face of death, and the pagan king is led to praise the living God whose kingdom never ends.
section.thesis: When loyalty to God is criminalized, Daniel prays as he always has, trusting God with the cost; God sends His angel to shut the lions' mouths, vindicating His innocent servant, so that the king proclaims the living God whose dominion will never end.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the plot and the trap of an unchangeable law; Daniel keeps praying openly; cast into the den under the king's seal; the lions' mouths shut and Daniel brought up unharmed; and Darius decrees praise to the living God.

units.label: The plot and the trap
units.note: a law that cannot be changed

verses.text: Now it pleased Darius to appoint 120 satraps to rule throughout the kingdom,
and over them three administrators, including Daniel, to whom these satraps were accountable so that the king would not suffer loss.
Soon, by his extraordinary spirit, Daniel distinguished himself among the administrators and satraps. So the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.

Thus the administrators and satraps sought a charge against Daniel concerning the kingdom, but they could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him.
Finally these men said, “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.”
So the administrators and satraps went together to the king and said, “O King Darius, may you live forever!

All the royal administrators, prefects, satraps, advisers, and governors have agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce a decree that for thirty days anyone who petitions any god or man except you, O king, will be thrown into the den of lions.
Therefore, O king, establish the decree and sign the document so that it cannot be changed, in accordance with the {{dath|law}} of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.”
Therefore King Darius signed the written decree.

units.label: Daniel keeps praying openly
units.note: just as he had done before

verses.text: Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, {{tsela|prayed}}, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before.
Then these men went as a group and found Daniel petitioning and imploring his God.

So they approached the king and asked about his royal decree: “Did you not sign a decree that for thirty days any man who petitions any god or man except you, O king, will be thrown into the den of lions?” The king replied, “According to the law of the Medes and Persians the order stands, and it cannot be repealed.”
Then they told the king, “Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, shows no regard for you, O king, or for the decree that you have signed. He still makes his petition three times a day.”

units.label: Cast into the den under the king's seal

verses.text: As soon as the king heard this, he was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel, and he labored until sundown to rescue him.
Then the men approached the king together and said to him, “Remember, O king, that by the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or ordinance established by the king can be changed.”
So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the den of lions. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!”
A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.
Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting. No entertainment was brought before him, and sleep fled from him.
At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the den of lions.
When he reached the den, he cried out in a voice of anguish, “O Daniel, servant of the {{elaha_chayya|living God}}, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?”
Then Daniel replied, “O king, may you live forever!
My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king.”
The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den, and when Daniel was lifted out of the den, no wounds whatsoever were found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

At the command of the king, the men who had falsely accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the den of lions, they and their children and wives. And before they had reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and crushed all their bones.
Then King Darius wrote to the people of every nation and language throughout the land: “May your prosperity abound.

I hereby decree that in every part of my kingdom, men are to tremble in fear before the God of Daniel: For He is the living God, and He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end.
He {{shezib|delivers and rescues}}; He performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions.”
So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

dath.gloss: A law, decree, or edict. The plot hinges on the dath of the Medes and Persians, a royal law that even the king cannot revoke. The unchangeable human decree is set against the higher law and living God to whom Daniel is loyal; the rigid edict traps the king but cannot bind God.

tsela.gloss: To pray, to bow in prayer. When the ban is signed, Daniel simply keeps on praying toward Jerusalem three times a day, just as before. His prayer is not defiance staged for show but steady, humble devotion that will not be interrupted by a royal threat.

elaha_chayya.gloss: The living God. Both the anxious king and the closing decree call the LORD the living God, in pointed contrast to the dead idols of gold and stone. He is the God who acts, who hears prayer, who shuts lions' mouths, and who endures forever while empires rise and fall.

shezib.gloss: To rescue, deliver, save. The same verb sounded through the fiery furnace now rings through the lions' den: God delivers and rescues, and He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions. It is the signature act of the living God, who saves His trusting servants.

basic.context: Under Darius, Daniel rises to the top of the government, and jealous rivals look for a way to destroy him. Finding him blameless, they trick the king into a thirty-day law that anyone who prays to any god or man but the king will be thrown to the lions. Daniel keeps praying openly toward Jerusalem, is caught, and is thrown into the den. God sends His angel to shut the lions' mouths, Daniel is found unharmed, and the king proclaims that the living God, who rescued Daniel, endures forever.
basic.hermeneutics: This famous story is the climax of the court narratives and a mirror of the fiery furnace. Daniel does not flaunt his prayer or provoke a fight; he simply refuses to stop worshiping God when worship is outlawed. His obedience shows the limit of loyalty to the state: we honor rulers, but we cannot obey a command to abandon God. God's deliverance is real, though as elsewhere in Scripture, faithful people are not always spared.
basic.originalLanguages: The trap is the dath, the unchangeable law of the Medes and Persians. Against it Daniel keeps up his tsela, his steady prayer. Both the frightened king and his final decree name the LORD the elaha chayya, the living God, over against dead idols; and the God who shezib, delivers and rescues, shuts the lions' mouths.
basic.typology: Daniel, innocent yet condemned, sealed in a pit under a stone, and brought out alive at dawn, is a striking picture of Christ, who was falsely accused, sealed in a tomb, and raised on the third day. The shut mouths of the lions foreshadow the defeat of death itself in the resurrection.
basic.christ: The innocent man cast into the pit and raised up unharmed points to Jesus, condemned though guiltless, laid in a sealed tomb, and raised to life. As God delivered Daniel from the lions, so God delivered Christ from death, and in Him delivers all who trust Him from the mouth of the grave. Christ is the living God who rescues His people.
basic.god: God is the living God who hears prayer and acts, who is stronger than lions, kings, and irreversible laws. He honors the faith of those who trust Him, sends His angel to protect them, and rules a kingdom that, unlike every human empire in this book, will never be destroyed. He is worthy of a worship no law can forbid.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 91 promises God's protection for those who trust Him. Acts 5 records the apostles saying we must obey God rather than men. And Hebrews 11 lists those who through faith shut the mouths of lions, with Daniel in view.
basic.oneStory: The last of Babylon's kings gives way to Persia, but God's servant is preserved and God's name is honored again by a pagan throne. The living God who rescues Daniel from the lions is the God who will rescue His people from death itself in Christ, and whose everlasting kingdom stands when all the empires of Daniel have crumbled to dust.

context.literary:
The chapter is a trap story built with great economy, and it runs in two matched movements divided at the sealing of the den. In the first half, verses 1 to 18, the pressure rises: the king plans to promote Daniel, the officials search for a flaw and find none, so they manufacture one, and the king is cornered by his own signature. In the second half, verses 19 to 28, the pressure is released in reverse order: the king rises at dawn, the prisoner speaks, the accusers are punished, and the decree of Darius ends where chapter 4 ended, in praise of the living God.

The verb 'to find' holds the plot together. The rivals look for a charge and cannot find one, verse 4, so they resolve to find something in his religion, verse 5. They then find Daniel praying, verse 11. In the den, Daniel says that he was found innocent in God's sight, verse 22, and that no wound was found on him, verse 23. The same word runs from the conspirators' failure to God's verdict.

The law of the Medes and Persians is repeated almost like a drumbeat in verses 8, 12 and 15, and the repetition is what makes the king helpless. Darius is not weak by temperament. He labours until sundown, verse 14, fasts, loses sleep and rises at first light, but a law written by himself stands above him. The mirror image is God, who is bound by nothing outside Himself and whose word actually stands.

The chapter also keeps a quiet symmetry with Daniel 3. There, a king's decree to worship an image is met by refusal, and the faithful are delivered from fire. Here, a king's decree to pray to no one else is met by faithfulness, and the faithful man is delivered from lions. Chapters 3 and 6 are the two great trials, and chapters 4 and 5 stand between them as the two lessons about kings.
context.historical:
Daniel is now an old man. He was taken to Babylon in the first deportation, Daniel 1:1, so he had served at court for some sixty-five years by the time Persia took the city. His age matters to the story: a man with decades of unblemished service is still the target of envy, and no record of faithfulness can protect him from a trap built out of his faith.

The administration described in verses 1 to 3 is typically Persian. The empire was divided into provinces governed by satraps, a Persian word, with higher officials set over them to protect the king from loss. Daniel's rise to the top of that structure is the same pattern as in Joseph and Mordecai: a foreigner whose competence makes him indispensable. The idea of an irrevocable royal edict appears elsewhere in Persian times, Esther 1:19 and 8:8, and Esther 8:8 shows how a law could not be revoked and had to be answered with a second decree. That is the same predicament Darius faces.

The prayer posture has a specific background. Solomon had prayed at the dedication of the temple that when his people were far away they would pray 'toward this place,' 1 Kings 8:30, and, in the land of their captors, 'in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers,' 1 Kings 8:48. Daniel's window opened toward Jerusalem is a deliberate act of obedience to that tradition, not a superstition about geography, and three times a day echoes the habit of the psalmist, 'Morning, noon, and night,' Psalm 55:17. Jeremiah's counsel to exiles to seek the welfare of the city, Jeremiah 29:7, helps explain why Daniel served well and prayed openly: he was a good citizen of Babylon and a worshiper of the LORD in the same breath.

The lions' den is consistent with the ancient Near East, where rulers kept lions and hunted them as a display of royal power. The identity of Darius the Mede remains debated, as discussed in the notes on chapter 5.
context.canonical:
The language of the story is steeped in the Psalms. The psalmist prays 'Save me from the mouth of the lion,' Psalm 22:21, and says 'my soul is among the lions,' Psalm 57:4. In Psalm 7:15-16 the person who digs a pit falls into it, and Proverbs 26:27 says the same, so the fate of Daniel's accusers is the working of a law written into God's order of things. Esther has the same shape: Haman is hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai, Esther 7:10, and the irrevocable royal decree there is answered by a second decree and not by repeal.

The book of Daniel itself makes the link to the earlier trials. In Daniel 3:17-18 the three friends say that God can deliver them and that even if He does not, they will not worship. Daniel 6 is the other half of that confession, with a man who is delivered and who gives God the credit. And Darius's closing decree takes up the language that Nebuchadnezzar used in 4:2, where he was 'pleased to declare the signs and wonders' of the Most High, and which is repeated in 6:27. The pagan throne becomes a pulpit three times in this book.

The New Testament names the story. Hebrews 11:33 lists those who 'through faith' 'shut the mouths of lions,' and in the very next verses the list turns to those who were tortured, flogged, and killed, Hebrews 11:35-38, so Daniel's rescue is set beside other faithful ones who were not rescued. Paul at the end of his life says, 'I was delivered from the mouth of the lion,' 2 Timothy 4:17. And Peter calls the devil a roaring lion looking for someone to devour, 1 Peter 5:8, which gives the den a second layer: believers face the lion not only in a pit but wherever they live.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author writes for people who must live under a government that does not share their God. His first aim is to answer the question of how: how a person can serve a pagan court with complete integrity and still worship the LORD without compromise. Daniel is not a rebel. His enemies had to admit that they could find no fault in him except in the law of his God, verse 5, and that admission is the author's argument. A faithful life is not a threat to the state unless the state forbids worship.

He also wants hearers to see where the line falls. Daniel does not change anything about his routine, verse 10, and the whole story turns on that detail. He does not escalate, preach at the king or organise resistance. He simply goes on praying in the way he always had, and the cost, if it comes, will come. The author wants the exiles to learn that conscience does not mean provocation, and that open fidelity in small daily habits is what keeps a person ready for the day of testing.

Third, the author wants his readers to know whose cause this is. The decree ends with the king commanding everyone to fear the God of Daniel. The deliverance is not for Daniel's reputation. It is a public sign to every nation and language that God is alive. The exiles are meant to read their own suffering in that light: they may be the place where God shows who He is.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes Daniel's deliverance; it does not promise that every believer who is thrown into trouble will come out unharmed. Daniel's own three friends had said 'even if He does not,' Daniel 3:18, and the New Testament knows of faithful people who did not escape, Hebrews 11:35-38. The story is one case of God's deliverance, and a witness that He can, but not a rule that He always will in this life.

What it does teach is by example. Daniel's practice, to pray three times a day, to give thanks as he prays, to pray openly without making a show of it, and to keep serving the state with honesty, is a pattern that the church is meant to learn. The principle that a believer obeys a human authority except where it requires disobedience to God, Acts 5:29, is drawn from the same ground, and sits alongside the call to honour rulers, Romans 13:1 and 1 Peter 2:13, and to pray for them, 1 Timothy 2:1-2.

The story does not command believers to seek out conflict, and the penalty on the accusers, which falls on their wives and children as well, is narrated and not recommended. Deuteronomy 24:16 shows that Israel's own law forbade punishing children for their fathers.

debates.question: Does Daniel's example justify disobeying the government?

views.label: Obedience is the rule; disobedience the narrow exception
views.case: Scripture calls believers to honor and submit to governing authorities, Romans 13; Daniel served the empire loyally and blamelessly, and disobeyed only the single command that forced him to stop worshiping God, showing that civil disobedience is limited to cases where the state commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands.

views.label: Faithful witness may accept the penalty rather than hide
views.case: Daniel does not flee, rebel, or even conceal his prayer; he keeps worshiping openly and is willing to bear the legal consequence, modeling a conscientious, non-violent refusal that submits to punishment while refusing to sin, as the apostles later do in Acts 5:29.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that loyalty to God is supreme and honor to rulers is real; the believer obeys the state in all things except where obedience would mean disobeying God, and then accepts the cost with a clear conscience.

debates.question: Why were the accusers' wives and children thrown to the lions?

views.label: Persian custom, narrated and not endorsed
views.case: The text reports the king's order without comment. Collective punishment of a family was known in the ancient world, and a similar scene appears when Haman's ten sons are hanged, Esther 9:13-14. On this reading the verse describes what a pagan court did and does not hold it up as a model.

views.label: A contrast with Israel's own law
views.case: Deuteronomy 24:16 says that fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers. Israel's law set a different standard from the Persian court. Some add that Achan and Korah, Joshua 7:24 and Numbers 16:27, show that the principle could be set aside by God in rare cases, but that this was never a license for kings.

debates.bearing: The narrator reports the king's act and moves on to the real point, God's vindication. Nothing in the chapter tells the reader to imitate it, and the standard to apply remains the one given in Deuteronomy 24:16.

debates.question: Does God always rescue the faithful?

views.label: Rescue is promised to those who trust Him
views.case: Psalm 91:11-13 says that He will command His angels to guard the one who trusts Him, and that such a person will tread on the lion. Daniel 6:23 says he was not harmed 'because he had trusted in his God.' Read together, they teach that trust in God is the way of safety.

views.label: Rescue is real but not guaranteed in this life
views.case: Hebrews 11:33 lists those who shut the mouths of lions, and in the same chapter, verses 35 to 38, others were tortured, flogged, stoned and sawed in two. Daniel's friends said in Daniel 3:18 that even if God did not rescue them, they would not bow. On this reading the faithful may be rescued from death or through it.

debates.bearing: The chapter shows that God can and does deliver, and that faith does not depend on knowing the outcome. Daniel prayed before he knew, and the New Testament sets both the rescued and the unrescued among the faithful.

study.originalLanguages:
Much of the force of the chapter lies in a few words and the way they repeat. The first is the word for the royal law. The king's ordinance is a 'statute' and the thing the officials ask him to establish is an 'interdict,' a prohibition with a penalty, repeated in verses 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 and 15. And the phrase translated 'cannot be repealed' in verses 8, 12 and 15 is literally a law 'which does not pass away.' That is exactly the verb used in Daniel 7:14 of God's dominion, which 'will not pass away.' Darius's law claims a permanence it cannot have, and the one who actually has it is the God whose kingdom is described in the very same terms. The human edict is called unchangeable; the divine kingdom proves to be.

The second is the language of devotion in verse 10. Daniel 'got down on his knees,' from the root that in Hebrew gives both the word for knee and the word to bless, and he gave thanks, using a verb from the root that gives the Hebrew words for thanksgiving and confession. The prayer is described in three layers: kneeling, asking and thanking. In verse 11 the men find him 'petitioning and imploring,' using a word for asking and a word that comes from the root of grace, as in the Hebrew word for a plea for mercy. Daniel is not demanding; he is asking to be shown favour.

The third is the word 'continually' in verses 16 and 20. Darius says twice that Daniel serves his God continually. The word carries the sense of constancy, an unbroken habit, and is the king's own testimony about the man he is about to condemn. A pagan king has seen that what Daniel does in private is what he does under threat.

The fourth is the verb 'found.' In verse 4 the rivals can find no charge, and the narrator reports it twice in different words. In verse 22 Daniel says that he was found innocent in God's sight, using a word for purity or innocence, a word for the declaration of a person's blamelessness before a court. The case of the officials fails because they could find nothing; the case of Daniel is vindicated by the court of heaven.

The fifth is the word for trust in verse 23. Daniel had 'trusted' in his God, and the Aramaic verb is the cousin of the Hebrew he'emin, the verb used of Abram in Genesis 15:6, where he 'believed the LORD.' It is a rare moment in the Aramaic section when the language of faith is used so plainly. Trust is the reason, in the narrator's mind, for the unharmed body.

Finally, the angel 'shut' the mouths of the lions, verse 22. The king has already closed the den with a stone and signet rings, verse 17, to keep Daniel in. God closes the mouths of the lions, to keep him alive. The same word, mouth, covers both: a stone over the mouth of the pit cannot hold back what the closed mouths of the beasts have already ended.

typology.type: The sealed pit and the morning, Daniel 6:17-19
typology.fulfillment: A stone is placed on the mouth of the pit, the king seals it with his ring, and the innocent man is shut in until the first light of dawn. The correspondence with the burial of Jesus is close and has been noticed since the early church: a stone, a seal, a guard, a night of waiting, and then the morning. Matthew 27:60 and 27:66 record the stone and the sealing of the tomb, and the women come 'very early in the morning,' Luke 24:1-2. The escalation is that Daniel was kept alive in the pit, while Christ went through death itself and rose. The type is an echo of rescue; the antitype is the resurrection.

typology.type: The king bound by his own law, Daniel 6:14-16
typology.fulfillment: Darius wants to save Daniel, and spends the day trying, but the law he signed stands above him. He is a ruler who loves a man whom he cannot free. The gospel answers that tension at the level of God's own justice. God is not bound by an outside law, but His own righteousness is the standard, and in the cross He acts 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26. Where Darius could only fast and wait, God satisfied the demands of the law Himself, since Christ was 'born under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5. The type falls short because Darius is helpless and God is not.

typology.type: The innocent man who intercedes, Daniel 6:10
typology.fulfillment: Daniel's habit of prayer, three times a day, with his face toward Jerusalem, shows a righteous man holding the city of God before God. Jesus is the greater pray-er: He often withdrew to pray, Luke 5:16, and knelt in the garden, Luke 22:41. Now at the right hand of God He 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25, and Romans 8:34 says He is interceding for us. Jesus also changes the direction of prayer: worship is no longer 'on this mountain nor in Jerusalem,' but 'in spirit and in truth,' John 4:21-24, because the temple toward which Daniel prayed is now found in Him.

typology.type: The accusers caught in their own trap, Daniel 6:24
typology.fulfillment: The men who dug the pit fell into it, the pattern spoken of in Psalm 7:15-16 and Proverbs 26:27. The cross shows the same reversal on a grander scale. The rulers who crucified Jesus did not understand what they were doing, 1 Corinthians 2:8, and the cross that was meant as a victory over Him became His, for God 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and triumphed over them by it, Colossians 2:15. Peter said that Jesus was handed over 'by God's set plan' and raised because death could not hold Him, Acts 2:23-24. The type is only a pattern of poetic justice; the antitype is the defeat of the powers.

study.christ:
The story leads to Christ most visibly through the pattern of the sealed pit and the morning, and the New Testament lets that pattern stand without forcing it. Jesus too was condemned by officials who could find nothing real to charge Him with, Pilate saying three times that he found no guilt in Him. He too was sealed in a place of death with a stone and a guard, Matthew 27:66. The night passed, and at dawn on the first day the stone was rolled away, Matthew 28:1-2. Daniel was preserved from death; Jesus passed through it, and that is the great difference. Where the king who put Daniel in the pit hurried to it at first light and cried out in anguish, the women come to the tomb at first light to find the stone moved and the one they sought alive. Daniel's rescue is a signpost; the resurrection is the road itself.

The story leads to Christ by the figure of the innocent one who suffers under an unchangeable law. Darius cannot undo what he has signed. The gospel tells us that God did not cancel His law by an act of power but fulfilled it, since 'God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law,' Galatians 4:4. The One who is just and the one who justifies are the same, Romans 3:26. The distance between the king's anguish and God's solution is the distance between a ruler who cannot save and a God who gives His Son.

It leads to Him by the pattern of faithful prayer. Daniel kneels three times a day and gives thanks. Jesus withdrew to pray, knelt in Gethsemane, and prayed 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. Where Daniel prayed in the face of a decree, Jesus prayed in the face of the cross. And the Jesus who prays is the Jesus who now 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25.

It leads to Him by the kingdom. Darius's final decree says that God's kingdom will never be destroyed and His dominion will never end. Daniel 7:14 gives the same words to the Son of Man, who receives that dominion. The kingdom that Darius confessed is the kingdom that Christ reigns in, and the 'living God' of verses 20 and 26 is the God who raised Jesus from the dead, Acts 2:24.

One caution applies. The lions are not a code for anything, and the angel who shuts their mouths is not Christ. The New Testament does not say that Daniel's story is a prophecy of the burial, and the links above work as echoes and not as proofs. They are strongest where the New Testament itself makes them: Hebrews 11 treats Daniel's deliverance as an example of faith, and Paul's own deliverance 'from the mouth of the lion,' 2 Timothy 4:17, is the experience of a servant who follows the same Lord.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the living God, and the proof is that He acts. Darius's question in verse 20 is the question of the whole book: 'has your God... been able to deliver you?' Idols cannot see or hear, Daniel 5:23, but this God hears prayer, sends an angel and shuts mouths. He is living in a way that makes a difference at dawn.

He is sovereign over the laws of men. The decree was unchangeable by every human standard and no one in the chapter, including the king, could revoke it. God does not have to repeal a law to save His servant. He works inside the sentence and brings His servant through it. The sentence stands, the lions are in the den, the stone is sealed, and the verdict of heaven prevails anyway. God's power does not need the permission of a government and is not hindered by its irreversibility. Daniel 2:21 says that He removes kings and establishes them, and Daniel 6 shows what that looks like when one of them has bound himself.

He is the God who knows innocence. Daniel says that he was 'found innocent in His sight,' verse 22. The accusers' case was constructed in human courts, with the law of a king; God's verdict was given in another court. This is a comfort for anyone who has been condemned unjustly: there is a Judge whose verdict stands even when a human one has been made.

He is a God who uses His enemies' plans to display Himself. The pagan king ends by writing a decree that tells every nation to fear the God of Daniel, and the plot that was meant to remove Daniel's faith publishes it throughout the empire. The same God who raised up Pharaoh to make His name known in all the earth, Exodus 9:16, uses Darius's law. He does not need the opposition, but He is never defeated by it.

He is a God of justice. The accusers are not spared, and the narrator does not apologise for the justice of the outcome. Yet it is not the justice the text approves, for the destruction of the wives and children is the king's act and not God's decree; the God of the Torah has said that each is to die for his own sin, Deuteronomy 24:16. The chapter holds God's justice and the king's excess apart.

Above all, He is the everlasting King, whose kingdom, in Darius's own words, 'will never be destroyed.' Every other power in this book is temporary and the God of Daniel is the one who remains. For worship, the chapter calls us to a steady habit, to kneel and give thanks at the window even when it costs, because the God who hears is the same in the den as at the table.

crossReferences.note: The three friends tell the king that God is able to deliver them, and that even if He does not they will not bow. Daniel 6 is the other trial in the book, and it supplies the delivered half of the confession while Daniel 3:18 keeps open the possibility that God might not deliver.

Solomon's prayer at the dedication anticipates the exile: if the people repent and pray toward the land, the city and the house, God will hear. Daniel's open window toward Jerusalem acts on this word, and shows the exile still reaching toward the place God chose.

The psalmist cries out in distress 'morning, noon, and night,' and says that God hears his voice. Daniel's three daily times of prayer fit this ancient rhythm of Israel, and show a man who prays as the psalms taught him, with thanks as well as need.

The wicked man digs a hole and falls into the pit he has made, and his trouble recoils on his own head. The destruction of Daniel's accusers in verse 24 is an example of the principle that God lets malice fall back on those who plan it.

The royal decree sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked, so a second decree is written to answer the first. Esther's story shows how Persian law worked and how God used it, as Daniel 6 does, to preserve His people without breaking the law.

Peter and the apostles say that they must obey God rather than men, when the council forbids preaching in Jesus' name. The principle that Daniel lived is stated plainly here, along with the willingness to take what follows, which in Acts is flogging and in Daniel is the den.

Among those who acted by faith, the writer counts those who 'shut the mouths of lions.' Daniel is clearly in view. The next verses add the faithful who were not rescued, so that the chapter holds deliverance and endurance as two forms of the same trust.

Paul, at the end of his life, tells of standing before authorities alone and says that the Lord stood by him, and that he was 'delivered from the mouth of the lion.' He uses Daniel's language for his own experience of the Lord's nearness, whether or not an actual lion is meant.

The chief priests ask for the tomb to be sealed with a stone and a guard so that the body cannot be stolen. The sealing of the tomb echoes the sealing of the den in Daniel 6:17, and in both the human seal is meant to settle the matter, and it does not.

The Son of Man is given a dominion that 'will not pass away,' using the verb that Daniel 6:8 applied to the unchangeable law of the Medes and Persians. Darius's law was never truly irrevocable; the kingdom of the Son of Man is.

Peter warns that the adversary prowls like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. The image makes Daniel's den a picture of the pressure every believer faces, and the answer is the same: be alert and stand firm, trusting the God who closes the mouths of lions.

study.oneStory:
The story belongs to the long account of how God's people live in a world they do not control. From Joseph in Egypt to Esther in Persia and Daniel in Babylon, the Bible tells of faithful servants who rise in pagan courts, are targeted because of their God, and are preserved so that the watching world can see who God is. Daniel 6 is the last of the court tales in the book, and its place is deliberate: after this, the book turns from stories of Daniel's survival to visions of kingdoms and their end.

It answers a question that goes back to the garden. Genesis 3 left humanity under the power of a serpent whose aim is to devour, and the Bible's later pictures call him a roaring lion, 1 Peter 5:8. In the den, the lions are shut up by an angel and the man they were meant to devour walks out. It is a small picture of the promise of Genesis 3:15 that the enemy will not have the last word.

It sets up the cross and resurrection with unusual clarity. Jesus was condemned by men who could find no real crime, sealed in a tomb by official authority, and brought out on the third day. The narratives share a shape because both belong to one purpose: the God who keeps His servants is also the God who raises His Son. Daniel was rescued from death's threat; Christ was rescued from death itself, and in Him believers are promised a resurrection, as Daniel 12:2 anticipates: 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake.'

The story also sets up the church's life. Believers in every age find that obedience to God can cost them under human law, and that God's deliverance may take the form of rescue or of endurance. The story gives hope that neither the law nor the lions are the last word.

And it ends in the new creation. The kingdom Darius confesses, which 'will never be destroyed' and whose 'dominion will never end,' verse 26, is the kingdom that Revelation shows when the nations bring their glory into a city that has no more curse and where God's servants worship Him. In that world there is no den, no sealed stone and no unrevokable decree of men, and the God who once shut the mouths of lions is the God who dwells with His people forever.

quiz.q: Why could Daniel's enemies find no ordinary charge against him?

options.text: He was trustworthy and blameless, with no corruption or negligence in his work.
options.note: Daniel 6:4 stresses his integrity; only his faith could be used against him.

options.text: He bribed the officials to stay silent.
options.note: The opposite; he was incorruptible, which is why they found nothing.

options.text: He hid his misdeeds carefully.
options.note: There were no misdeeds to hide; he was found blameless.

options.text: The king protected him from all scrutiny.
options.note: They investigated him thoroughly and still found nothing.

quiz.q: How did Daniel respond when the decree against prayer was signed?

options.text: He kept praying toward Jerusalem three times a day, just as he always had.
options.note: Daniel 6:10 shows steady, unbroken devotion, not a staged protest.

options.text: He stopped praying for thirty days to stay safe.
options.note: He did not stop; he continued praying as before.

options.text: He prayed secretly where no one could see.
options.note: He prayed openly at his window, just as he had done before.

options.text: He fled the kingdom to avoid the law.
options.note: He stayed and kept worshiping, ready to bear the cost.

quiz.q: How was Daniel delivered in the den?

options.text: God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and Daniel was unharmed.
options.note: Daniel 6:22 credits God's angel with shutting the lions' mouths.

options.text: The lions had already been fed and were not hungry.
options.note: The text attributes the rescue to God's angel, not to well-fed lions.

options.text: Daniel fought off the lions with his hands.
options.note: He did nothing but trust God, who shut the lions' mouths.

options.text: The king pulled him out before the lions arrived.
options.note: Daniel spent the night among the lions, kept safe by God.

quiz.q: What did King Darius decree after Daniel's deliverance?

options.text: That people everywhere should fear the living God of Daniel, whose kingdom will never end.
options.note: Daniel 6:26-27 records his praise of the living, eternal God.

options.text: That Daniel should be executed after all.
options.note: The opposite; he honored Daniel and praised his God.

options.text: That prayer to any god should be banned permanently.
options.note: He reversed course, commanding reverence for the God of Daniel.

options.text: That the lions should be worshiped.
options.note: He directed worship to the living God who rescued Daniel.

quiz.q: How does Daniel in the den point us to Christ?

options.text: An innocent man sealed in a pit under a stone and brought out alive at dawn foreshadows Christ's death and resurrection.
options.note: The pattern anticipates the sealed tomb and the risen Lord, Matthew 27:66 and Acts 2:24.

options.text: It teaches that faithful people are always kept from physical harm.
options.note: God did deliver Daniel, but the deeper pointer is to Christ's resurrection, not a guarantee of safety.

options.text: It shows that lions can be tamed by brave men.
options.note: The rescue was God's act; the point is God's deliverance, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The innocent one sealed in a pit and raised at dawn clearly foreshadows Jesus.

questions: Daniel's enemies could find nothing against him except his faith. If people searched your life for a charge, would only your devotion to God stand out?
When prayer was outlawed, Daniel simply kept doing what he had always done. How settled and regular is your own life of prayer, before any pressure comes?
Daniel honored the king yet would not obey a law that forbade worshiping God. Where might you face a choice between pleasing people and staying faithful to God?
Daniel trusted God with the outcome, whether he lived or died. How does the promise of resurrection free you to obey God even when it is costly?
A pagan king ended up praising the living God because of one faithful life. How might your quiet faithfulness become a witness to those who hold power over you?

translationNotes.note: The law of the Medes and Persians was famed as unalterable once issued, which is why even the king cannot rescind the decree that traps Daniel.
Praying toward Jerusalem, three times a day, reflects the practice of facing the temple, as in Solomon's prayer, 1 Kings 8:44-48.
God sent His angel, the same language as the fiery furnace, marks the deliverance as God's direct act on behalf of His innocent servant.
The final line may be read as the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus, or as the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus, bearing on the identity of Darius the Mede.
